summary: Ponderosa-pine tree lookout in Sisters, OR, built 1921 with a 105-foot platform; sources conflict on whether it ended in 1926 or 1934.

facts.design: Tree lookout: a ponderosa pine with iron steps and a small enclosed platform at the top (register calls it a 105-foot crow's nest)
facts.status_note: Central Oregonian says it was cut down after use ended in 1926; the register gives removal in 1934 and firelookout.com says destroyed that year

events.note: Built by the Forest Service as a 105-foot tree lookout one block east of the present ranger station (register) or just north of the district office (Central Oregonian)
Central Oregonian: remained in use until 1926, when rot set in and it was cut down
Register says removed; firelookout.com says destroyed. Conflicts with the 1926 cut-down date in the Central Oregonian

evidence.supports: built 1921 as a 105-foot crow's nest one block east of the ranger station; removed 1934
evidence.quote: Built in 1921 one block east of the present ranger station, this 105' crows nest was removed in 1934.
1921: 105' crows nest. Located 1 block east of present ranger station. Destroyed 1934.

evidence.supports: location in Sisters, Deschutes County, Oregon
constructed by the Forest Service in 1921
evidence.quote: The tower was constructed by the Forest Service in 1921.

evidence.supports: 105 feet high with a small platform at the top
evidence.quote: It was 105 feet high and had a small platform at the top of the tree.

evidence.supports: ponderosa pine with limbs removed and ladder steps up the trunk
evidence.quote: It was a large ponderosa pine tree that had the limbs removed and ladder steps constructed up the trunk of the tree.

evidence.supports: iron steps arched up the trunk
evidence.quote: The steps were made of iron and shaped like an arch
The platform at the top had three sides enclosed and was approximately 3 feet by 3 feet.

evidence.supports: located just north of the present Sisters Ranger District office
evidence.quote: It was located just north of the present Sisters Ranger District office.

evidence.supports: used by Forest Service and state forestry to search for fires, especially after thunderstorms
evidence.quote: The lookout was utilized by the Forest Service and the Oregon State Forestry Department to search for forest fires in the Sisters vicinity particularly after thunderstorms.

evidence.supports: staff did not like the climb and spent hours on the platform
evidence.quote: Men staffing the lookout were not eager to climb up and down the ladder and often spent several hours sitting in the small platform at the top of the tree.

evidence.supports: wind made the tree sway, prompting a quick descent
evidence.quote: If it became windy, the tree would sway several feet and led to a quick descent from the platform.
The Sisters lookout remained in use until 1926 when it began to show signs of rot and had outlived its usefulness.

evidence.supports: remnants of old tree lookouts remain in some trees on high points; climbing them is ill-advised
evidence.quote: Remarkably there are still some trees on high points of local forests that have remnants of the old tree lookouts, but it would be an ill-advised to attempt to climb them today.

sources.title: Sisters Ranger Station Fire Lookout Tower
Sisters Lookout briefly stood as an unusual structure

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Central Oregonian says the lookout was used until 1926 and then cut down; the register gives removal in 1934 and firelookout.com gives destruction in 1934. Both dates are reported in the story; the sources do not agree and none is corroborated.

Register and firelookout.com say one block east of the present ranger station; Central Oregonian says just north of the present Sisters Ranger District office. Record coordinates (44.2918, -121.55314) were kept; they match the register.
Register calls it a 105-foot crow's nest; Central Oregonian describes a pine tree with iron steps and a small platform. Treated as one structure described two ways.

notes_for_editor: The 1926 vs 1934 end date is the main open point, and the Central Oregonian article is the only source with a 1926 date. A 1996 Nugget 'Recollections of Sisters' article turned up in search: it is about the Black Butte cupola and 1934 CCC tower, not this lookout, so it is not cited. A Deschutes Historical Museum post and a Facebook comment thread also show 1921 and 1934 in search snippets only; their text was not read, so they are not cited. No source describes the site today, and access is unknown.
